title: Leaders Who Unintentionally Intimidate Others
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece examines leaders whose intensity and status intimidate others without any intent to do so, and the cost of that dynamic: team members who withhold feedback, bad news, and pushback. It argues that trying to strip away the traits that built a leader's success is nearly impossible, so the better strategy is to add offsetting behaviors rather than subtract the intense ones. Chief among those offsets is a visible willingness to help, admit mistakes, and say 'I don't know.' The conclusion reframes the fix as addition, not transformation.
points: Leaders can intimidate others simply through status and intensity, without any intent to do so.
Intimidated team members withhold feedback, pushback, and bad news, making the leader less effective.
Trying to strip away deeply ingrained intense traits is nearly impossible for most leaders.
The recommended fix is to add offsetting behaviors — helping others, admitting mistakes — rather than change core style.
A willingness to say 'I don't know' is highlighted as one of the most effective softening behaviors.
quotes: Good leaders don’t purposely want to intimidate people, but too often they accept the fact that they overwhelm others without trying to dampen the negative effects their style has.
Those who feel intimidated are reluctant to raise issues, offer feedback, push back, or elevate bad news.
The many elements that create intimidation are usually exceedingly difficult to change, alter, or replace.

In addition to admitting their mistakes and being quick to say, “I don’t know,” nothing softens an intimidating style as much as a willingness to lend a hand and provide unconditional support for those who follow.
Sometimes we don’t need to change our style as much as we need to add to it.
